articles.title: Postman silently auto-installs AI plugins and attempts to share all API data
articles.summary: Postman silently auto-installs AI plugins and attempts to share all API data

top_comments: It's a shame what happened to Postman. It started as an excellent little developer tool for testing APIs. Then for some reason they raised over $400M in funding and hired 1,500+ employees, for what should have been a tiny OSS/passion project like curl or little snitch. Instead they now have to justify their valuation by forcing logins, collecting data, monthly subscriptions, AI features, etc.I still don't know how they're valued at $5B+ when I don't know a single developer who actually uses it anymore

Postman logs detailed information on every single API request you make through its tool, including query parameters. If you use the templating syntax `{{some_secret}}` to fill in a query parameter, it sends the actual secret content of `some_secret` to Postman's servers. If you disable outgoing network traffic to this logging endpoint, the entire app will stop working properly.I discovered this when investigating whether Postman is HIPAA-compliant (it is not).
Who still uses Postman? In my experience it became insanely slow and bloated. Switched to Bruno. IMO, Postman is like uTorrent, everybody heard about it and many install because of inertia.

articles.title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
articles.summary: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too

top_comments: Not making any claims about a specific model's capabilities, but all these "can interpret model weights" posts brings to mind the line in Shakespeare's Henry IVGLENDOWE: I can call spirits from the vasty deep.HOTSPUR: Why, so can I, or so can any man, but will they come when you do call for them?I can interpret weights too, but will that interpretation be correct?

Qwen-3.8-27B - the best thing that happened in AI so far.This thing can accomplish the same results as the frontier models do, if you are willing to play a role of an higher level architect or decision maker. Guide it a bit here and there like a tech lead and you get everything done.The money you pay for frontier models is exactly for outsourcing that high level direction work to agents.

Perhaps I’m missing this, but can Qwen 3.8 alter Qwen 3.8 weights?There are a lot of known neurons in the older Qwen models that are long known to induce behaviour changes (see evil Qwen by changing one weight).My question boils down to how much is trained vs being able to actually understand the weights. Presumably a same gen model isn’t trained on any sources dissecting that generation. And how much do longer known conceits like steering vectors, J spaces, LoRAs play into this?This doesn’t explain the game training cases, which are very impressive to me.

articles.title: Stringman, an $800 open-source room scale gripper robot
articles.summary: Stringman, an $800 open-source room scale gripper robot

top_comments: Hi there, I'm Nathaniel, the creator of this robot. Thanks for posting it :) If you have any questions feel free to ask.Can it kill you? no probably not. The tension limit kicks in and lets the line out if you pull too hard.Will it work in a room with a ceiling fan? usually its fine since you can lower the work area ceiling to exclude the fan.Will it make my kids learn to not pick up after themselves? They never will anyways.

I made a big one for my garden. It is like a that scene in honey i shrunk the kids with Rick Moranis laying in that cantilevered flying cot thing but i use 2 high speed winches and some machined aluminum and the cabling sort of like an etch a sketch controls. I control it with the same usb gamepad that titanic sub imploded with. i can raise and lower myself about 4 feet to get inbetween the rows. It is pretty fun to play in too. I want to build a robot to get in it and then remotely control the whole thing. Its basically the same thing as the NFL spider cam but holds more because I'm a fatass and performs much worse. I used 12 foot 4x4s with concrete bases. Its about a 20 feet by 35 feet garden. My only real concern is the longevity of the cables, the hight im suspended at isn't really dangerous but i know i am not using the right cables for the winch. 3/16 in marine grade vinyl coated 4200 pound working load limit. my spools or whatever you want to call it is 6 inches im afraid theres too much tension on parts sometimes. I had an alternate design that used water as a ballast and you just pump or drain water to move around the grid but that was too ambitious for my lazy ass.

It's an interesting concept, but I think I'll hold out for the full-body humanoid version.There is an undeniable allure to the idea of a bipedal chassis realizing I'm an inefficient drain on corporate resources, then stabbing me to death while I sleep due to a minor Terms of Service violation.

articles.title: Safari introduces Adaptive Dark Mode in 27.3
articles.summary: Safari introduces Adaptive Dark Mode in 27.3

top_comments: FYI, light-dark() in CSS is a thing now.https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/V...
I want the opposite. I suffer from astigmatism, which makes white on black hard to read. I wish Safari could turn dark mode websites into light mode websites.

I use dark mode for everything, so I'm pretty happy about this. Some sites were clearly designed to be light, and forcing dark on them could break the experience, but that's exactly what `color-scheme: light only` is for, and it's good that Safari respects it. Other than that it feels like a win-win to me: great for dark mode users, and for devs not much changes, you just add "light only" if you don't want your site to be affected.

articles.summary: The Little Book of Generative AI Foundations: An Intuitive Mathematical Primer

top_comments: I don't like:> Changing coordinates. Given a vector x expressed in the standard basis, we change coordinates by applying x_eig = V^−1 x. > This operation does not change the vector itself; it only changes how the vector is represented, converting it into eigenvector coordinates.I'm sure the author knows about the difference between the vector and a coordinate vector given a basis. I just don't like this wording. It's weird to say applying a function doesn't affect a change.

Another book which I would highly recommend for learning the math (or at least getting a very good idea of how it works) behind machine learning/transformers is "Why Machines Learn: The Elegant Math Behind Modern AI" by Anil Ananthaswamy. I read it this past year and I found it was extremely good at pacing and building up intuition to the "how and why" of most important math concepts and discoveries in ML that have lead to where we are today. For those who don't already have a fairly deep understanding of linear algebra, statistics, and multivariate calculus, this book will be a far more gentle introduction yet still has enough rigor for you to come away with something.
Wow, this book is surprisingly readable! I like how he starts from basics of linear algebra.

As someone who writes high-reliability C++ but is completely outside the standards process, I see the issues with C++ Contracts. It isn’t clear that it solves a problem that anyone has in real codebases, especially after C++20 concepts.If you were already writing high-reliability C++ then the benefits are difficult to quantify. If you weren’t writing high-reliability C++ then it saves you almost nothing over doing the standard idioms of high-reliability C++ that were already available to you at very marginally more cost. It does standardize expression of it in narrow cases but the payoff seems minimal.Most of what C++ Contracts delivers is a mashup of what you can already do with constexpr and C++20 Concepts. I like reliability features but this feature, as delivered, looks fairly useless if you already use reliability features. A compelling standard would need to make much deeper guarantees out of the box. And the compiler can already see through most compositions of constexpr and C++20 concepts, which is already very expressive.C++ Contracts looks a bit like a feature that was designed long before current standard features existed.

While I can understand that C++ contracts were met with controversy, contract annotations scoped at analysis time that can be verified by external tools, such as static analyzers, model checkers, or automatic theorem provers, are incredibly useful.I put together an alternative function contract and invariant mechanism in C using CBMC and custom macros that effectively allows me to perform formal methods in C using compositional verification. The reason why I chose C is because of its relative simplicity and relative ease of building tooling around it. C++ contracts provide some feature parity, and would let me take advantage of some of the features in C++ relative to C.I hope that the contract proposal is workshopped and simplified so it can be proposed again for a future version. Its current form is unsuitable, but it deserves a second chance with a simpler implementation. Contracts would narrow the safety gap between C++ and languages such as Ada / SPARK.

This article makes it sound the options are normally approval, rejection and abstention, but that this time round a fourth option, "disapproval", was reached. It that the case, or are they just trying to say that people rejected it?

I always find so much cognitive dissonance in these kinds of posts.> My most successful work this year was hand-writing a tool, replacing ~4,000 lines of vibe-code with a few hundred. My system has proven more flexible, easier to test, and more generalizable than what it replaced.> agents still need human taste and experience to produce good work.Where do you think human taste and experience in software comes from?> overstimulating & exhausting in a way that coding never was.> for many of us, honing the code, finding the right design, seeing the parts mesh together — that was the meditative purpose we found in our jobs.> That’s not the only time AI waylaid me. LLMs could not figure out how to annotate that model’s training data correctly. I spent days going back and forth with them> LLMs are not yet good companions when brainstorming complicated things.Why do we expect this to get better? The training data will degrade in quality if more people rely on LLMs so I'd expect models to eventually start getting worse even if they currently enjoy apparent improvements in output.> Writing code is solved.What a strange thing to say given all the above experiences, which I think we all share.Why are we willing to give up so much in terms of purpose and understanding for perceived productivity gains?

There is no substitute for reading the code in many many cases. I spend more than 3k/mo on tokens. I find incorrect assumptions baked into the code (the ultimate spec) and missed by the agents and tests daily. This is more pronounced in data analysis and complex systems.As a side effect having to read the code at least once inevitably makes it way shorter and usually much better.

I believe that anyone who says that writing code is no longer needed, was probably not a very good coder to begin with. I have seen what the best models can do, and I've seen what people call "good", and I am not impressed.However, I'm still split. Because this could mean that we see a jump in code quality, due to bad coders getting someone better to code for them. But we could see a decrease in code quality, due to less people "caring".
